episode_title: Leadership, learnings and the publishing landscape - Richard Bogie - Ep 43
question: What was Richard Bogie's first advertising sales role and when did he join the newspaper industry in 1986?
transcript_excerpt: Richard Bogie saw a job at The Guardian, phoned up a recruitment consultancy, got an interview about a week later, and by the end of that day had a job at The Independent, which was a newly launched newspaper at the time. He joined in June of 1986 after graduating, when the advertising sales department had not yet been built and there were many empty desks.

episode_title: Leadership, learnings and the publishing landscape - Richard Bogie - Ep 43
question: How did Richard Bogie manage a team of over 200 people and millions in advertising sales targets at Express Newspapers?
transcript_excerpt: When Bogie became Group Sales Director at Express Newspapers at age 32-33, he had 200 people in regional offices as well as London with complex revenue streams. He realized he was just managing managers with potentially two or three layers of them, and worked with a great team including Andy Janesko who promoted him. He focused on making decisions, asking for help, learning from mistakes, and motivating teams toward a common cause. Over five years at Express, revenue increased every year through adding new offerings like internet products and sports sponsorship teams.

episode_title: Leadership, learnings and the publishing landscape - Richard Bogie - Ep 43
question: What publications did Richard Bogie manage during his time at IPC in the 1990s?
transcript_excerpt: At IPC, around age 27-28, Bogie oversaw a centralized classified sales department and had Enemy, Melody Maker, and Loaded under his management, along with Marie Claire, Options, TV Times, Women's Weekly, and a collection of yachting and sailing titles including Horse and Hound and Country Life.

episode_title: Leadership, learnings and the publishing landscape - Richard Bogie - Ep 43
question: Why did Richard Bogie leave Future Publishing after nine months and join Express Newspapers?
transcript_excerpt: Bogie spent nine months at Future Publishing (which had been acquired by Pearson) and found it was not a particularly happy period. Pearson tried to Pearsonize Future Publishing, but Future Publishing had grown as a renegade organization that worked to its own rules, and Pearson found it did not fit their portfolio. He received a phone call to join Express Newspapers under new management when Lord Hollick had bought it from Lord Stevens, and he was drawn to the charismatic sales director Andy Ginesco, deciding 'I want to work for this guy.'

episode_title: Leadership, learnings and the publishing landscape - Richard Bogie - Ep 43
question: How did News UK's recruitment process for the Scotland General Manager role result in Richard Bogie getting hired in 2015?
transcript_excerpt: Three different people told Richard Bogie that News UK was looking for a general manager for Scotland and had put him forward, but no phone call, email, or approaches came. Bogie looked up the name of the fellow at News UK leading recruitment and sent him an email saying he was interested in the job. The fellow came back straight away, and six interviews later Bogie had the job. Later over a drink, the recruiter told him Bogie had been on their list but they thought he was happy in his job and wasn't going anywhere, so they had put him aside.

episode_title: Leadership, learnings and the publishing landscape - Richard Bogie - Ep 43
question: What changes did Richard Bogie make to his work schedule after becoming Managing Director of News Scotland and News Ireland?
transcript_excerpt: Richard Bogie now works three days a week instead of his previous full-time schedule managing both Scotland and Ireland. He is in Dublin once or twice a month (previously two days a week for three weeks of the month), London once or twice a quarter (previously every two to three weeks), Glasgow two or three days a week, and Edinburgh about a day a week. He now focuses more on strategy, trade organizations, political engagement, online harms, freedom of information, platform challenges, and AI rather than hitting weekly or quarterly commercial numbers.
